name: The Belvoir Oak
species: Oak (Quercus robur or Quercus petraea, species not established)

location.address: Belvoir Park Forest, near the Motte, off the Outer Ring Road (A55) car park, Belfast BT8

access: Free. Forest Service NI managed forest park, open 24 hours, car park off the Outer Ring Road (A55); also reachable via the Lagan towpath from Shaw's Bridge or the Galwally Avenue entrance.
transport: Galwally rail halt (Lagan Valley line) approx 15 min walk; several Translink bus routes serve Outer Ring Road / Milltown Road nearby.
verify_notes: Widely called 'possibly the oldest oak in Ireland/Northern Ireland' and 'Granddad'. Ancient Tree Forum (ancienttreeforum.org.uk) gives ~500 years, grid ref J338696, 'open to the public', managed by Forest Service NI. DAERA's own 2023 news page (government source) calls it 'believed to be the oldest living oak in Ireland, 500 to 600 years old, dating back to the 1500s' and used it to front a 2023 oak photography exhibition at the forest, which is the most recent dated evidence of life found (3 years old). Irish News (2016, quoting Dan Clarke, senior ranger, Lagan Valley Regional Park) puts a different figure on it: 'more than 400 years old, exact age cannot be accurately determined due to the tree's condition', girth 'just under 9 metres', and describes it as severely deteriorated ('barely has enough branches or twigs') yet still producing six acorns that winter, which the ranger called remarkable. Local History Videos (localhistoryvideos.com) adds that the tree survived a 2014 Phytophthora ramorum (sudden oak death) outbreak that felled roughly 25% of Belvoir Park Forest's trees, and says it 'survives thanks to the intervention of tree specialists'. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: remarkabletrees.org (Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees project) states explicitly that the tree historically photographed by Robert Welch over a century ago (then already 'well over 300 years old') and known locally as 'Granddad' may NOT be the same specimen as the tree currently promoted as 'The Belvoir Oak' (nominated for Woodland Trust Tree of the Year 2023) -- i.e. there may be two distinct veteran oaks in the forest near the motte, one seriously declined ('Granddad', 9m girth per 2016 report) and one healthier and more publicly promoted since. Could not resolve which is which from available sources within the pass; flagging this as the single biggest open question for a future pass or a reader with local knowledge. Species is given only as 'oak' everywhere found; not confirmed to Quercus robur vs petraea. Location: grid reference J338696 exists (Ancient Tree Forum) but I did not trust my own Irish Grid to WGS84 conversion enough to mark this confirmed; pin here is the forest/Motte area (park-level), not the individual trunk. A future pass with mapping tools should convert J338696 properly and/or find a geotagged photo to upgrade this to confirmed.
girth_source_note: Girth figure (~880cm, 'just under 9 metres') is from the 2016 Irish News article about 'Granddad'; if that is a different tree from the currently-promoted 'Belvoir Oak', this girth may not belong to the same individual. Recorded anyway per the standing rule to always capture girth when a source gives it.

name: The Grass Tree of the Palm House

location.address: The Palm House, Belfast Botanic Gardens, College Gardens, Belfast BT9 6BQ

access: Free entry to the gardens; the Palm House itself is open daily, 10am to 4pm April to September, 10am to 3:45pm October to March.
transport: Botanic rail halt approx 5 min walk; several Metro/Glider bus routes stop on Botanic Avenue/University Road nearby.
verify_notes: Not a tree in the usual sense (Xanthorrhoea is an Australian monocot 'grass tree', family Asphodelaceae, not a true tree), but it is the oldest living specimen at Belfast Botanic Gardens and a genuine oddity worth flagging to the writer to frame honestly rather than presenting as a conventional tree. Three independent sources (Wikipedia's Botanic Gardens Belfast page, connollycove.com visitor guide, elitetravelblog.com) agree: over/approximately 400 years old, arrived in Belfast during Queen Victoria's reign (1837-1901), housed inside the 1840s cast-iron Palm House (foundation stone 1839, wings completed 1840, dome added 1852 per fobbg.co.uk, the Friends of Belfast Botanic Gardens' own site). Most concrete dated 'alive' evidence found is that it survived a major 2005 renovation of the Palm House; several tourism pages written in the 2020s describe it in the present tense as a current fixture of the glasshouse, but no dated 2020s sighting/photo was found in this pass, so flagging the recency gap per the alive-now bar. Species given specifically as Xanthorrhoea preissii by elitetravelblog.com. Location is confirmed at the Palm House building level (a small, single glasshouse), not to the exact pot/bed inside it. No girth or height figure found or applicable in the usual sense.

name: The Dawn Redwood by the Kelvin Statue

location.address: Belfast Botanic Gardens, near the Kelvin statue by the Malone Road entrance, Belfast BT9

access: Free. Belfast Botanic Gardens, open daily during daylight hours.
transport: Botanic rail halt approx 5 min walk; several Metro/Glider bus routes stop on Botanic Avenue/University Road nearby.
verify_notes: Historically significant rather than genuinely ancient: Metasequoia glyptostroboides was known only from fossils and presumed extinct until living specimens were found in China in 1946; seed grown at the Arnold Arboretum (Boston) in 1948 supplied the first plants distributed to botanic gardens worldwide, including this one. Friends of Belfast Botanic Gardens (fobbg.co.uk, the gardens' own volunteer/education body, cites a specific tag: 54deg34.985'N, 5deg56.156'W, Tag #59) date this specimen to approximately 1950, making it one of the first dawn redwoods grown in Ireland after the species' rediscovery -- a 'living fossil' story worth leading with. The Tree Council of Ireland's register (treeregister.ie) also lists a Dawn Redwood at Belfast Botanic Gardens, corroborating it as a recognised notable specimen, though its own page gave no extra measurement detail beyond the listing itself. Two other Metasequoia specimens stand elsewhere in the same gardens (rock garden; beside the Malone-gate-to-Palm-House path) if this one needs replacing or a photo cannot be matched confidently -- note that risk explicitly for the photo pass. A WebSearch AI summary claimed a monumentaltrees.com height of 22m for this tree, but monumentaltrees.com 403'd every direct fetch attempt in this pass (expected, they block automated fetching) so that figure was NOT verified on the page itself and is deliberately excluded per the search-summary-is-a-lead-never-a-source rule. Age is estimated from the planting/distribution history (documented planting era for the species' UK/Ireland introduction), not from a girth measurement.

name: The Friar's Bush Hawthorn
age_estimate: not documented; described as old and reclining

location.address: Friar's Bush Graveyard, Stranmillis Road, Belfast BT9, beside the Ulster Museum

access: Free, but appointment-only: Belfast City Council manages the graveyard and visitors must book ahead (call 028 9027 0296 or email the council) to be let in; guided tours also run through Cairde na Cille and Friends of Friar's Bush Graveyard. No car parking on site; some paths unsuitable for wheelchairs.
transport: Metro 8A-B from Belfast city centre, alight at Botanic Gardens; Botanic rail halt also nearby.
verify_notes: The graveyard itself IS the story here: this is the oldest Christian burial ground in Belfast and gives the site its name. Two independent sources agree on the core legend: remarkabletrees.org (Northern Ireland's Remarkable Trees project) and Belfast City Council's own page both say Catholics gathered secretly to hear Mass under this hawthorn during the Penal Laws of the 18th century (Mass being banned), which is why the graveyard is called 'Friar's Bush'. Wikipedia independently corroborates via a citation to poet Joseph Campbell's verse calling it the 'Stranmillis trysting thorn'. remarkabletrees.org adds a specific (if unverifiable) origin legend: a friar was supposedly murdered and buried on the spot near the thorn where he preached, and a stone marked the grave. Council's own page says the tree stands 'in the centre of the cemetery'. Species given as hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna, the common native hawthorn) by remarkabletrees.org; no scientific name given by the other two sources but nothing contradicts it. No numeric age or girth found anywhere; described only as 'old' and 'reclining' (remarkabletrees.org: 'may well bow down under the weight of its history'), consistent with a genuinely veteran, low, spreading hawthorn rather than a tall tree. IMPORTANT ACCESS NOTE: this is NOT casual walk-up access. Belfast City Council's own page states visitors must make an appointment (phone or email) to get in; this is publicly-owned and free but gated, not open-gate public ground. Flagging for the writer/owner to judge against the current access rules for a bookable/appointment site (allowed as of the 2026-09-01 loosening as long as the access line states it plainly, which I have done). No dated recent (2020s) sighting confirming the specific tree is still alive was found in this pass; the graveyard is actively managed and toured (Cairde na Cille, Friends of Friar's Bush Graveyard both currently active per Council's page), which is indirect but real evidence the site and its named feature are still being shown to visitors.
